ctx.x: Your father, and your mother, even though they were into music, still wonder about your choice. Did they have an attitude, pro or con, about jazz in itself?

No, they didn’t have a problem with jazz, because I was very lucky with them, I came from that era of black — there’s that word again — of black families, that stressed a couple of things you and I talked about before. First it was education. They come from that sort of Martin Luther King era where education is your way out, which they imparted that to me and it sticks with me and I still think, and as I study and try to help other people and help myself I realize that by increasing the quality of the product or…

items.title: Byron Stripling interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 25, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: during the Montgomery bus boycott one of the things Martin Luther King did during that period of time is he said before I speak... we’re going to sing for like twenty minutes.

ctx.x: Okay. Well it’s a little ironic, I was thinking about last November for some reason was a particularly bad month for me and my cohorts gig-wise. And now those are the good old days.

Oh gosh. Yeah. You know it’s up to, the hardest part about being an artist or a musician I think is the creation, the continuous creation of art and we have to look at this time as that’s another part of the gift, to get ourselves physically together, that’s why I try to walk as much as I can every day. We’ve been doing about two miles a day. Not a lot and I should do more. You know and try to eat right. But then getting down into making yourself better as an artist — all that stuff that you want to give to…
